Article Title: Colorado veteran Cano Espinoza began covering his home with discarded hubcaps, cans, screen doors and scrap metal in 1980; more than four decades later, Cano's Castle remains a well-known roadside att
Article Text:
The castle had stood in their neighbourhood for years, becoming part of the town's identity.

A castle of discarded materials

The castle suffered serious damage when a fire broke out in January 2022

When fire destroys Cano's Castle

Residents recall growing up around the castle

In the small town of Antonito in southern Colorado, United States, a house made from discarded beer cans, hubcaps, screen doors and scrap metal became a well-known roadside attraction. According to The Denver Gazette, called Cano's Castle, the structure was built by Dominic “Cano” Espinoza, a Native American Vietnam War veteran who reportedly began working on it in 1980.The personal construction project eventually became a local landmark. Espinoza used materials that others had thrown away, combining them with native volcanic stone to build a complex that stood out from the surrounding homes. Over the years, the unusual structure attracted visitors and became familiar to people living in Antonito, a small town near the New Mexico border.The castle was also Espinoza's home. Known locally as a private man who often travelled around town on his bicycle, he continued to be closely associated with the property. His religious faith was another part of his identity, according to reports about the castle and its builder.However, on January 13, 2022, a major fire damaged the property. The blaze destroyed the residential section of the complex, although Espinoza escaped without injuries. The incident raised concerns about a structure that had been part of the town for more than four decades.Espinoza reportedly began building Cano's Castle in 1980, using a combination of volcanic stone and materials collected from discarded items. Not relying entirely on conventional building materials, he incorporated objects such as old hubcaps, metal scraps, screen doors and beer cans into the structure.The beer cans were carefully cut and used as part of the castle's exterior. Along with the other metal objects, they gave the building its distinctive appearance. The complex also featured two tall towers known as the King and the Queen.Located on a residential street, the property was not a conventional castle. It was a collection of structures created from salvaged materials, reflecting the work Espinoza had carried out over several decades.His project became known as a form of folk art, a term used for creative work often made outside formal artistic institutions. Cano's Castle attracted attention because of the materials used in its construction and the amount of work involved in creating it.For residents of Antonito, the building was more than an unusual roadside sight. It had stood in their neighbourhood for years, becoming part of the town's identity.The castle suffered serious damage when a fire broke out in January 2022. The fire was reported shortly after midnight, and firefighters from Antonito, Romeo, Manassa and La Jara responded to the incident.Emergency crews continued fighting the flames until around 5 am. The main fire was extinguished by late morning, although smaller flare-ups were reported afterwards.Antonito police officer Olga Cortez confirmed that the fire had destroyed the residence within the complex. However, the castle's two prominent towers, the King and the Queen, were not damaged. Espinoza was the only occupant of the property at the time and was not injured.The cause of the fire was under investigation when the incident was reported. Cortez said it might have started in the chimney, although this had not been confirmed.She also said Espinoza had not been fully cooperative with authorities following the incident. Describing his reaction to the damage, Cortez said, “He’s more upset.”The fire affected people who had known the castle since childhood. Among them was Alex Ponce, who lived in an apartment across the street with his girlfriend and son.Ponce told The Denver Gazette that he woke up to see large flames coming from the property. At first, he believed strong winds were causing the beer cans attached to the structure to make noise. He soon realised that the sound was connected to something far more serious.Having been born in Antonito, Ponce had grown up seeing the castle and had even toured it as a child. Watching the property burn was particularly difficult because it had been a familiar part of his surroundings for so many years.“It’s heartbreaking,” Ponce said by phone, “to see something you’ve known all your life go up in flames.”He also expressed confidence that the local community would come together to help Espinoza rebuild his home and the work he had spent decades creating.Although the January 2022 fire destroyed Espinoza's residence, the castle's two main towers survived. According to a report published by OnlyInYourState in 2023, Espinoza continued living on the property in an off-grid trailer. A later report by The Denver Gazette, in July 2025, continued to describe Cano's Castle as a roadside attraction. It is not confirmed whether fire-damaged residence had been rebuilt.
Article Summary: Cano's Castle was built by Dominic ‘Cano’ Espinoza in 1980. He used materials such as hubcaps, metal scraps, screen doors and beer cans. The structure became a roadside attraction in Antonito, Colorado. On January 13, 2022, a major fire damaged the property. The blaze destroyed the residential section of the complex, but the two main towers survived.

Article Title: In 2024, Glenn and Barbara Britt left Dartmouth at least $150 million; the gift nearly doubled its zero-parent-contribution income threshold from $65,000 to $125,000 and expanded Tuck scholarships
Article Text:
The donation also marked an important development for Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business, where Glenn Britt completed his MBA in 1972.

Donation changed financial aid at Dartmouth

The announcement came years after Glenn Britt's death in 2014

Tuck School of Business

Who were Glenn and Barbara Britt?

In March 2024, Dartmouth College in the United States announced that it would receive more than $150 million from the estates of former Time Warner Cable CEO Glenn Britt and his wife, Barbara Britt. The donation, the largest bequest dedicated entirely to scholarships in Dartmouth's 255-year history, was intended to make education more affordable for students from middle-income families. It also provided additional scholarship funding for students at Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business.According to the college, the gift allowed Dartmouth to nearly double the annual family income threshold under which parents are not expected to contribute towards their children's undergraduate education. The limit increased from $65,000 to $125,000 for families with typical assets. Dartmouth said the revised threshold was the most generous of its kind in the United States at the time.Under the arrangement, three-quarters of the donation was allocated to undergraduate financial aid, while the remaining quarter was set aside for scholarships at Tuck. The new policy was scheduled to take effect in the 2024–25 academic year, covering eligible students already enrolled at Dartmouth as well as incoming members of the Class of 2028.The announcement came years after Glenn Britt's death in 2014. Barbara Britt died in August 2023. Dartmouth said the exact value of their bequest would be determined once their estate was fully settled, although the college and Tuck were assured of receiving at least $150 million.Before the Britts' donation, Dartmouth did not require a parental contribution from families earning $65,000 or less annually, provided they had typical assets. The bequest raised that income threshold to $125,000, extending the benefit to more middle-income households.According to Dartmouth, the change was expected to provide financial relief to approximately 350 families each year across its four undergraduate classes.However, zero parent contribution does not mean students have no financial responsibility. Under the policy, eligible students are still expected to contribute money earned through summer jobs and employment on campus. Dartmouth said this student contribution would not exceed $5,000 annually.The change built on Dartmouth's existing financial aid policies. The college had already introduced need-blind undergraduate admissions for applicants regardless of citizenship, committed to meeting 100% of demonstrated financial need and replaced required undergraduate loans with expanded scholarships.Speaking about the donation, Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock said, “Glenn Britt credited Dartmouth for transforming his life, and he was tremendously grateful for the financial aid award that made his Dartmouth experience possible.”She added, “This remarkable bequest from Glenn and Barbara ensures that, regardless of background, the dream of a Dartmouth education can become a reality.”The donation also marked an important development for Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business, where Glenn Britt completed his MBA in 1972.Dartmouth described the portion allocated to Tuck as the largest single outright gift in the business school's history. The funding was intended to establish long-term scholarship support through the Britt Scholars programme.The scholarships were designed to help Tuck attract talented students, including those facing greater financial difficulties. Dartmouth specifically highlighted first-generation students, who accounted for 19% of Tuck's Class of 2025.Matthew Slaughter, then dean of Tuck, said the scholarships would continue supporting deserving students in the couple's names.“Having a cohort of Britt Scholars in perpetuity will ensure we continue to provide a life-altering Tuck education to the most deserving students, in Glenn’s and Barbara’s names,” he said.Glenn Britt grew up in Nyack, New York, in a family of modest financial means. He attended Dartmouth with the help of a substantial financial aid award and graduated in 1971 with a degree in economics.During college, he participated in the marching band and worked at the student radio station, WDCR. He later earned his MBA from Tuck and joined Time Inc., beginning a career in telecommunications.Britt became president of Time Warner Cable in 1999 and CEO in 2001. During his tenure, the business grew from a $6 billion division into an independent publicly traded company generating $21 billion in annual revenue.Barbara Britt, meanwhile, studied history at Douglass College, then the women's college at Rutgers University. She worked as a journalist and photographer for Time's in-house publication, FYI. The couple married in 1975.Both supported educational and cultural organisations, including the Manhattan Theatre Club. Barbara also remained involved in conservation, animal welfare and educational outreach.Glenn Britt maintained a relationship with Dartmouth long after graduating. He supported the college financially, volunteered as an admissions ambassador and served on the Tuck Board of Advisors.The couple also supported technology education through Tuck's Glassmeyer/McNamee Center for Digital Strategies. Their Britt Impact Technology Series introduced students to developments in technology and related career opportunities.
Article Summary: Donation changed financial aid at Dartmouth. Announcement came years after Glenn Britt's death in 2014. Three-quarters of the donation was allocated to undergraduate financial aid, while the remaining quarter was set aside for scholarships at Tuck. The new policy was scheduled to take effect in the 2024–25 academic year.

Article Title: UC San Diego biologists identified the genetic switch that gave butterflies an extra light-detecting cell in their eyes, expanding their colour vision beyond imagination
Article Text:
The researchers found that butterflies did not redesign their entire visual system. Instead, they effectively duplicated one component of the existing arrangement, adding a second R7 photoreceptor to each eye unit.

The eye that broke the mould

Recreating the butterfly eye

A brain already waiting

Evolution in the making

A butterfly's world is not simply brighter or more colourful than ours. It is built from a richer visual vocabulary, one shaped by an evolutionary tweak hidden deep inside its compound eyes. While most insects have spent hundreds of millions of years working with a familiar visual blueprint, butterflies took a different route, adding an extra light-sensing cell to every tiny visual unit. Now, researchers at the University of California San Diego have identified the genetic switch that made this unusual upgrade possible.According to the UC San Diego website, compound eyes are made up of hundreds of tiny units, each containing a cluster of photoreceptors that detect light. In most insects, including flies, each unit contains eight such cells, arranged in a remarkably conserved pattern. Butterflies are different. Their eye units contain nine photoreceptors, giving them access to a broader range of colour information. The advantage can be particularly useful when navigating flowering plants, finding nectar and locating potential mates.Scientists in Michael Perry's lab at the UC San Diego School of Biological Sciences traced this difference to a surprisingly specific genetic change.Their study, published in Science Advances, focused on painted lady butterflies, one of the world's most widespread butterfly species. The researchers found that butterflies did not redesign their entire visual system. Instead, they effectively duplicated one component of the existing arrangement, adding a second R7 photoreceptor to each eye unit.The discovery became even more striking when the researchers tested whether this genetic alteration alone could produce the additional cell. They introduced the relevant genetic change into fruit flies, activating a gene in cells where it is normally switched off and doing so during the short developmental window when the eye is forming, adds the report.The result was a fruit fly whose individual eye units developed nine photoreceptors rather than the usual eight, following what the researchers described as a butterfly-like arrangement.But creating an additional light detector raised another evolutionary puzzle. A new sensory cell needs somewhere to send its information. If the eye had acquired an extra photoreceptor, surely the brain would also have needed to evolve a new neural connection to process its signals.The researchers discovered that the fly brain already produces more neurons than it ultimately needs. Cells that fail to establish useful connections normally disappear during development. When the experimental flies developed an extra photoreceptor, some of these otherwise surplus neurons were recruited to connect with it. They survived and established the appropriate wiring without requiring another genetic innovation.The finding suggests that evolution can sometimes exploit biological flexibility that already exists rather than having to build an entirely new system from scratch.The researchers also identified a hawkmoth displaying what may be an intermediate stage in a similar evolutionary transition. The lower portion of its eye contains two R7-like cells in each unit, resembling the butterfly arrangement, while the upper portion retains the single-cell configuration typical of flies. That uneven pattern could offer clues about how such a major visual change spreads through an eye during evolution.The next question is whether the additional photoreceptor actually gives the engineered flies the richer colour perception associated with butterflies. Testing that could reveal whether adding a single sensory cell is enough to transform how an animal experiences its surroundings.For now, the discovery offers a rare look at evolution working with an existing toolkit: one genetic switch, one extra sensory cell and a brain surprisingly prepared to make use of it.Images Courstesy: UC San Diego website
Article Summary: Butterflies added an extra light-sensing cell to every tiny visual unit. Scientists at the University of California San Diego identified the genetic switch that made this upgrade possible. The finding suggests that evolution can sometimes exploit biological flexibility that already exists rather than having to build an entirely new system from scratch.

Article Title: A $100 million gift from Stephen and Denise Adams made Yale School of Music tuition-free; for 2026-27, admitted students receive a full-tuition award worth $42,000 plus a school fellowship
Article Text:
Apart from helping students financially, the couple's contributions supported improvements to Yale's music facilities

$100 million donation changed Yale

Both Stephen and Denise Adams also served as members of the Yale School of Music's Board of Visitors.

What financial assistance do students receive?

Donation also supported new music facilities

Students admitted to the Yale School of Music in the United States receive a full-tuition award and a fellowship, thanks to a $100 million donation made by Stephen Adams and his wife, Denise Adams, in 2005. The contribution allowed the school to remove tuition fees for its students, a policy that continues more than two decades later.The donation was initially made anonymously, and the couple's identities were not publicly revealed until 2008. According to Yale, the money not only made tuition-free education possible but also helped improve academic programmes and facilities at the school.For students pursuing graduate studies in music, tuition fees can be a major financial burden. A November 2005 report by The Washington Post described how students at leading American music conservatories often had to take on debt or give music lessons to meet their tuition and living expenses. The Adams donation was intended to change this situation at Yale.The school's current financial aid policy states that all admitted students receive a full-tuition award and fellowship, except those who have received awards from other agencies.However, students may still need financial assistance for living expenses and other fees. Yale provides information about federal loans, student employment and additional grants to help them manage these costs.The donation was not the first contribution Stephen and Denise Adams had made to Yale. In 1999, the couple gave $10 million to the School of Music to mark Stephen Adams' 40th reunion. At the time, it was the largest contribution the school had received.Their much larger donation followed in 2005. The $100 million gift enabled the school to provide tuition-free education to its students and strengthen its educational programmes.Interestingly, Stephen Adams developed his interest in music relatively late in life. According to Yale, he began playing the piano as a hobby when he turned 55. The experience encouraged him to support music education.“That sparked my interest in music and I made the decision soon after to give the first gift,” Adams told the Yale Daily News in a 2009 interview.Although the couple initially chose to remain anonymous, their contributions later became publicly associated with the school's development. Both Stephen and Denise Adams also served as members of the Yale School of Music's Board of Visitors.According to the Yale School of Music's financial aid page, admitted students receive a full-tuition award and a fellowship, subject to the exception for students holding awards from other agencies.This means that eligible students do not have to pay tuition fees for their studies at the school. However, tuition-free education does not necessarily mean that every expense associated with studying at Yale is covered.The school separately provides information about loans that students can obtain to meet living expenses and other fees. Students may also explore employment opportunities available through Yale's student employment programme.Financial aid information is available for both US citizens or permanent residents and international students. The school's website also provides details about additional financial support, including the Belding Fund and the Student Relief Fund.Apart from helping students financially, the couple's contributions supported improvements to Yale's music facilities.In September 2013, Yale announced that its music complex, centred around the renovation and expansion of Hendrie Hall, would be named the Adams Center for Musical Arts. The announcement was made by School of Music Dean Robert Blocker and Yale President Peter Salovey during Convocation. The couple had also pledged another $10 million towards the renovation of Hendrie Hall.At the time, Blocker acknowledged the impact of their contributions, saying, "The extraordinary gifts of Denise and Stephen Adams have transformed the School of Music and Yale University. Their philanthropy has enabled us to make our dreams realities, and to advance the cause of music and cultural leadership throughout the world."The renovation projectincluded improved rehearsal facilities, faculty studios, practice rooms and a common space for students.Hendrie Hall housed Yale Opera, the School of Music's brass and percussion departments, and the Yale Philharmonia library. It also provided offices and practice facilities for undergraduate musical organisations, including the Yale Bands, Yale Glee Club and Yale Symphony Orchestra.
Article Summary: Stephen and Denise Adams donated $100 million to the Yale School of Music in 2005. The donation allowed the school to remove tuition fees for its students. The money also helped improve academic programmes and facilities at the school. In September 2013, Yale announced that its music complex would be named the Adams Center for Musical Arts.

Article Title: A washing-machine-sized NASA supported spacecraft will approach four defunct satellites and rocket bodies, testing technology that could one day help repair spacecraft or remove orbital debris
Article Text:
Otter will travel to within hundreds of yards of each object and examine it without making physical contac

How will spacecraft inspect objects in orbit?

How will Otter travel between different objects?

Why is NASA testing this technology?

Who is behind the SSPICY mission?

A spacecraft about the size of a washing machine is preparing to approach objects that are no longer working in Earth's orbit. The mission, supported by NASA , will test whether a spacecraft can independently navigate towards inactive satellites and rocket bodies, examine their condition and move between different orbits. The technology could eventually help repair spacecraft or remove unwanted objects from space.The mission, called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY), was launched on October 1 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. It involves a spacecraft named Otter, developed by US-based company Starfish Space. According to NASA, Otter will approach up to four inactive space objects of US origin in low Earth orbit, including satellites and rocket bodies.The inspections are expected to begin in early 2027. During this phase, Otter will travel to within hundreds of yards of each object and examine it without making physical contact. Much of the navigation will be handled by the spacecraft's own software, with minimal assistance from controllers on Earth.The mission is not intended to repair satellites or remove space debris immediately. Instead, it will test several technologies together to determine whether they can support such operations in the future.NASA says this will be the first time these capabilities are demonstrated as an integrated system.Approaching an inactive satellite is different from approaching one that is still operating. A spacecraft that is no longer functioning may be spinning or positioned in a way that makes it difficult for another spacecraft to approach safely.To carry out the inspections, Otter will use autonomous guidance and control software. This means the spacecraft will be able to make navigation decisions without waiting for instructions from ground controllers at every stage.Its computer vision system and sensors will help it observe nearby objects and determine how to approach them. The software will use this information to make navigation decisions in real time as Otter moves closer to its targets.During each inspection, the spacecraft will collect information about the object's spin rate, orientation and surface condition. Spin rate refers to how quickly an object rotates, while orientation describes the direction in which it is positioned. Examining the surface will provide information about its physical condition.These observations are important for understanding how a future spacecraft might safely approach an object that is no longer under active control.The SSPICY mission will also demonstrate how a small spacecraft can move between objects travelling in different orbits.Otter is equipped with an electric propulsion system that will allow it to travel between inspection targets. The mission will test how this system works alongside other technologies needed for precise movement in space.Another important component is an articulating robotic boom. This movable structure will be used to test the positioning of the spacecraft's thrusters, which provide the force needed to change its movement.By adjusting the direction in which the thrusters point, the spacecraft will test precise manoeuvring between different orbits.NASA says the combination of electric propulsion, autonomous navigation, sensors and the robotic boom is central to the demonstration. Although these technologies have different functions, the mission will examine how they perform together during a series of close approaches.The mission comes as increasing numbers of satellites are being launched into Earth's orbit. Thousands of satellites are launched each year to support services such as communications, weather forecasting and navigation.However, satellites and rocket bodies can remain in orbit after they stop working. Objects that experience problems or are no longer in service may collide with one another or break apart.Such incidents can produce orbital debris, ranging from large fragments to much smaller particles. These objects create concerns for spacecraft operating in the same environment.NASA is therefore supporting technologies that could make it possible to inspect inactive objects before attempting more complicated operations.For SSPICY, the immediate objective is inspection rather than removal. Otter will not touch or dock with any of the four targets during the mission.However, the technologies being tested could eventually support spacecraft servicing and repairs. They could also help future missions remove unwanted objects by pulling them into Earth's atmosphere for disposal.Starfish Space developed and operates the Otter 24C spacecraft being used for SSPICY. The company has also prepared the spacecraft for the technology demonstration at its facilities in Seattle.NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems programme, which operates under the agency's Research and Technology Mission Directorate, is funding and managing the demonstration.The agency's Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programmes also provided funding awards to Starfish Space during the early development of the spacecraft's key technologies.The inspections planned for 2027 will help demonstrate whether these systems can work together during autonomous close approaches. While SSPICY will not carry out repairs or debris removal itself, the results could help develop future missions capable of performing those tasks in orbit.
Article Summary: The mission, called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY), was launched on October 1 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. It involves a spacecraft named Otter, developed by US-based company Starfish Space. Otter will approach up to four inactive space objects of US origin in low Earth orbit, including satellites and rocket bodies. The inspections are expected to begin in early 2027.

Article Title: In 1967, an Australian man built a house from thousands of discarded glass bottles; nearly 60 years later, the unusual Lightning Ridge building survives as a mining museum and tourist attraction
Article Text:
The Bottle House was built in 1967 and remains one of the distinctive landmarks in Lightning Ridge.

How discarded bottles became building material

The building's walls are its most distinctive feature. Rows of glass bottles form the structure, giving it an appearance unlike a conventional house made with bricks, timber or concrete.

From a miner's camp to a museum

Today, the building houses a small museum featuring objects linked to opal mining and minerals.

Where visitors can see the Bottle House

The attraction offers a look at both the region's mining heritage and an unusual approach to construction.

Thousands of discarded glass bottles became the building material for an unusual house in the Australian outback in 1967. Nearly six decades later, the structure still stands in Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, where it serves as a tourist attraction and a museum displaying opal-mining artefacts, vintage bottles and other historical objects. Known as the Bottle House, the building was constructed by Tex Moeckel. Its walls are made from glass bottles fixed together, while its sharply pitched, almost A-frame roof is covered with corrugated iron. Inside, the building has several small rooms and a loft.According to the official website of the New South Wales government, the Bottle House was built in 1967 and remains one of the town's distinctive landmarks. It also lists it as the Bottle House and Mining Museum, describing it as an example of unusual architecture and resourcefulness in a former mining camp.The Bottle House was created using bottles collected from Hebel, a small town across the Queensland border. According to the New South Wales Government's official tourism information, the bottles were initially joined using cement. Moeckel later discovered that local clay was more suitable because it made it easier to replace a bottle if it broke. The building's walls are its most distinctive feature. Rows of glass bottles form the structure, giving it an appearance unlike a conventional house made with bricks, timber or concrete.Light passing through the glass creates another visual feature, highlighted in the official tourism website's photo gallery. The available historical records do not specify the exact number of bottles used in the construction. However, the building's walls are made almost entirely from bottles, making discarded glass the defining element of its design.The Bottle House was originally associated with a miner's camp, reflecting Lightning Ridge's history as an opal-mining settlement. The town, in northern New South Wales, is widely known for its black opals and has a long history of mining and small-scale settlement. As reported by The Lightning Ridge Historical Society, Dave Martin operated the Bottle House for a period during the 1970s. An advertisement for the attraction appeared in the local Lightning Flash newspaper in September 1969, indicating that it was being promoted to visitors soon after it was built.Today, the building houses a small museum featuring objects linked to opal mining and minerals. Visitors can also see a collection of vintage bottles, artworks and other old items. The collection extends beyond the bottles incorporated into the walls, giving the attraction a broader connection to local history.The Bottle House and Mining Museum is located on Opal Street in Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, postcode 2834. According to the New South Wales Government's website, the listed admission price ranges from 2 to 10 Australian dollars (AUD). Visitors who need accessibility information are advised to contact the venue before visiting. The attraction offers a look at both the region's mining heritage and an unusual approach to construction. Its glass-bottle walls remain the main draw, while the mining artefacts and vintage objects provide additional context about the area.Built in 1967 by Tex Moeckel, the Bottle House has survived as a reminder of a time when discarded materials were used to create a distinctive local building. It now serves a different purpose from its early days as part of a miner's camp: preserving and displaying pieces of Lightning Ridge's history for visitors.
Article Summary: The Bottle House was built in Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, in 1967. Its walls are made from glass bottles fixed together, while its sharply pitched, almost A-frame roof is covered with corrugated iron. Today, the building houses a small museum featuring objects linked to opal mining and minerals.

Article Title: Meet T’Emi Oshin, the 20-year-old Wayne State student who scored 1590 on the SAT and became the university’s first Obama-Chesky Voyager Scholar; she is also being honoured for youth advocacy and publi
Article Text:
Oshin's commitment to advocacy began during her school years in Midland. As a junior at H.H. Dow High School, she founded the Black Student Alliance after conversations with fellow Black students revealed a need for greater connection and a safe space to discuss their experiences.

A first for Wayne State

Finding her voice through community

Academic excellence with a wider purpose

A new chapter in public service

For T’Emi Oshin, medicine was never simply about what happens inside a clinic. Long before college, the Midland native imagined herself becoming a doctor. But as she grew older, science, public health and community work broadened that ambition, showing her that improving lives can begin well before a patient reaches an examination room. At 20, Oshin is now a junior at Wayne State University, studying public health and neuroscience while preparing for medical school, states an online report by Midland Daily News. Alongside her academic journey, she has built a record of youth advocacy and community leadership that has recently earned her two significant honours. Scroll down to read about her journey.In September, Oshin was selected for the 2026-28 class of Obama-Chesky Voyager Scholars, becoming the first student from Wayne State University to receive the public service scholarship, states the online report.The programme offers financial support, mentorship and funding for a summer work experience that scholars design themselves. Oshin plans to use the opportunity in 2027 to learn from youth-led organisations in other communities, exploring how young people are tackling challenges around them and what barriers they face.The scholarship comes at a point when Oshin is increasingly interested in the space between medicine and public policy.She hopes to become a physician, with primary care and paediatrics among the areas she is considering, but she is also curious about the role of nonprofits and government in creating healthier communities, adds the report.As per the report, Oshin's commitment to advocacy began during her school years in Midland. As a junior at H.H. Dow High School, she founded the Black Student Alliance after conversations with fellow Black students revealed a need for greater connection and a safe space to discuss their experiences.The initiative grew beyond simply creating a community for students. Members gave presentations to younger students about Black history and related subjects, turning the group into a platform for education and engagement. Oshin later helped establish Black Youth of Midland, bringing young people from different schools together for monthly meetings at the Midland Area Community Foundation. Her introduction to philanthropy also came through the foundation's Midland Area Youth Action Council. The experience helped shape an interest that has since become an important part of her work.Oshin's academic record has been equally striking. She graduated from Dow High in 2024 and was named one of 625 semifinalists in the U.S. Presidential Scholars Program, selected from more than 6,000 candidates nationwide. She also earned a 1590 on the SAT, one of the highest scores associated with Dow High. At Wayne State, she is part of the BS/MD Med-Direct programme, combining undergraduate education with a pathway toward medical school, adds the online report.Her interest in public health developed during high school as she became more aware of how factors outside a doctor's office can influence health outcomes. That perspective has particularly drawn her toward Black youth mental health and the broader conditions that shape young people's wellbeing.Oshin's growing list of accomplishments has now added another distinction. On November 18, she is scheduled to receive the Outstanding Young Philanthropist award at the National Philanthropy Day Awards Luncheon at Saginaw Valley State University. The Midland Area Community Foundation nominated her for the honour.Behind the awards is a network of teachers and mentors who helped nurture her interests, from science educators and STEM mentors to advisers who supported her youth advocacy efforts.For Oshin, the next chapter appears to be less about collecting achievements and more about understanding how those achievements can translate into service. Whether that eventually takes her into a clinic, a nonprofit, government or a combination of all three, her goal remains rooted in the same idea that shaped her ambitions as a child: using knowledge to make life better for others.Images Courtesy: Midland Daily News
Article Summary: T’Emi Oshin is a junior at Wayne State University, studying public health and neuroscience while preparing for medical school. Alongside her academic journey, she has built a record of youth advocacy and community leadership that has recently earned her two significant honours. In September, Oshin was selected for the 2026-28 class of Obama-Chesky Voyager Scholars, becoming the first student from Wayne State to receive the public service scholarship. On November 18, she will receive the Outstanding Young Philanthropist award.

Article Title: An Arkansas family treated the same fence as its property line for nearly six decades; after new neighbours removed fencing and trees, an appeals court upheld $12,000 in treble damages and an order to
Article Text:
The fence became more than just a fence

Tree removal resulted in $12,000 damages

The fence must be rebuilt

A fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties, after a dispute over trees and fencing reached the state Court of Appeals. The ruling in Floyd v. Bowlin-Lemon, reported by Justia, Leagle and Case Law Wire, affirmed the Bowlins’ boundary claim, a $12,000 treble-damages award and an order requiring the neighbouring owners to rebuild the fence. The case involved adjoining properties in Crawford County and centred on a fence line that the Bowlin family had treated as its southern boundary for decades. According to the Arkansas Court of Appeals, Joy Bowlin-Lemon’s family acquired the property in 1967. The family was shown the existing fence lines when it purchased the land and subsequently used those fences as practical boundaries. The property was used for livestock, including cattle and horses, while the family also maintained the land up to the fence by brush hogging and cutting hay.That arrangement remained unchallenged for decades. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property.The court record says portions of the longstanding fence were removed beginning in 2017, with the fence eventually torn down. Trees in the disputed area were also cut down. The Bowlins eventually filed a lawsuit in 2023, alleging trespass and destruction of their fencing and trees. A Crawford County Circuit Court trial followed in October 2024.The central legal question was whether years of treating the fence as the boundary could establish a legally recognised boundary even if the fence did not precisely match the surveyed property line. The appeals court said yes.Under Arkansas law, a boundary by acquiescence can arise when neighbouring landowners tacitly accept a particular line as the dividing boundary for a long period. The court noted that an express agreement is not required, nor does there need to have been an earlier dispute over the property line.In this case, the decades of maintenance and use along the fence, combined with the absence of objections from neighbouring owners, provided sufficient evidence for the lower court’s decision. The court also noted that the southern fence extended roughly 30 to 40 feet beyond the surveyed property line. Despite that discrepancy, the long-established conduct surrounding the fence supported its recognition as the boundary.The dispute also became costly for the Floyds. The circuit court determined that the trees removed from the disputed area were worth $4,000. The Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld that valuation, finding that testimony about the number and type of trees, photographs of the property and evidence of the clearing provided enough support.The court also upheld treble damages, bringing the total award to $12,000. Arkansas law allows treble damages when someone cuts, destroys or removes trees belonging to another person. The appeals court found enough evidence to support the finding that the tree removal was intentional or, at minimum, sufficiently reckless or negligent to trigger the statute. Among the evidence considered was the presence of no-trespassing signs along the fence and Ty Floyd’s admission that he removed trees and portions of the fencing.The lower court also ordered the Floyds to rebuild fencing along the eastern and southern boundaries. The appeals court left that order intact. It noted that Ty Floyd had indicated during the trial that he was willing to rebuild the fence, while his attorney did not object when the Bowlins requested the injunction.That meant the Floyds could not later challenge the fence-rebuilding requirement on appeal. There was, however, one issue the appeals court sent back to the circuit court. The original judgment did not contain a sufficiently precise legal description of the boundary. The appeals court therefore remanded the case for the limited purpose of adding a specific description that would allow the established boundary to be identified directly from the judgment.The decision underscores how decades of conduct can matter in property disputes. A fence may begin as a practical marker, but when generations of adjoining owners consistently treat it as the dividing line, that conduct can ultimately carry legal weight, even when a later survey points somewhere else.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments box below.
Article Summary: Fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property. The Bowlin family had treated the fence line as its southern boundary for decades.

Article Title: ‘The Orange Plague’: Why a golden, naked Trump is sitting on another man
Article Text:
File photo: Visitors looks at a scupture titled "The Orange Plague" by Danish artist Jens Galschiot

What does the statue symbolise?

Why is Trump depicted naked?

Why has the statue been installed at the European Parliament?

Where else has ‘The Orange Plague’ been displayed?

A 2.6-metre-tall statue of US president Donald Trump, naked and coated in 23-karat gold leaf, has been installed inside the European parliament in Strasbourg, France.Titled ‘The Orange Plague’, the sculpture by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt depicts Trump sitting on the shoulders of a frail, smaller man, with his thighs and sagging belly wrapped around the man’s head. Trump holds a golf club in one hand and the scales of justice in the other. The work is also known as the “King of Injustice”.The sculpture is a satirical critique of what Galschiøt sees as Trump’s threats to the environment, international cooperation and the rules-based world order. The artist has said the US president is destroying the causes and institutions he believes in, including efforts to tackle climate change. The work also questions how political power is exercised and how its consequences are borne by those with less power.The smaller man beneath Trump represents the burden imposed by the powerful on the less powerful.A plaque at the base of the sculpture captures the imbalance through the words: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except step down from his back.”The imagery suggests a leader who claims to help others while continuing to place the weight of his power and decisions on them.The golf club and scales of justice add to the political satire, juxtaposing Trump’s personal image with the idea of justice. Its gold finish is also a deliberate choice: Galschiøt has pointed to Trump’s fondness for gold, saying he believes the president might even like the sculpture.Galschiøt has said the sculpture draws inspiration from Danish author Hans Christian Andersen’s fairy tale ‘The Emperor’s New Clothes’, in which a vain emperor parades through his city naked while those around him pretend he is wearing magnificent clothes.This is also not the first Trump sculpture to depict Trump naked based on a correlation with the fairy tale, a previous series of statues displayed across the US by an artist collective was also titled, ‘The Emperor Has No Balls’.By depicting Trump naked, Galschiøt seeks to ridicule the president and strip away the image of authority surrounding him. “Dictators don’t like you laughing at them,” the artist said, explaining the thinking behind the work.Galschiøt is known for provocative political art. His best-known works include the Pillar of Shame, a memorial to victims of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre that was controversially removed from a Hong Kong university in 2021. He has drawn a parallel between the two works, saying both concern the relationship between the powerful and the powerless.The exhibition was sponsored by Danish politician Per Clausen, a member of the European parliament’s left-wing group, The Left. Members of the European Parliament are entitled to sponsor cultural events and exhibitions on parliamentary premises, subject to approval by officials. The sculpture’s installation therefore does not amount to an official endorsement of its message by the European Union.Clausen said he wanted to encourage debate about how power is used around the world and how Europe can protect its interests without becoming dependent on Trump. He defended the exhibition as an opportunity to display work that not everyone might agree with.Galschiøt, who had feared the application would be rejected, viewed the approval as an opportunity to bring criticism of Trump into the European Parliament. He said many Europeans regard the US president’s conduct as a serious problem, even if they recognise that he is the leader of an important ally.The sculpture has previously been displayed at the Munich Security Conference and the COP30 United Nations climate conference in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025. It was also shown at demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier in 2026 calling for Greenland to be protected from US ambitions.The Strasbourg installation was accompanied by 3D-printed miniature versions of the sculpture, distributed to visitors as “protest tokens”. The artist has said he produced around 20,000 miniatures for distribution to visitors and European Parliament staff.The temporary exhibition in Strasbourg is expected to remain on display until Thursday. Galschiøt plans to exhibit the sculpture again at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, next month. Trump has not publicly commented on the artwork.
Article Summary: Sculpture by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt depicts Trump sitting on the shoulders of a frail, smaller man, with his thighs and sagging belly wrapped around the man's head. Trump holds a golf club in one hand and the scales of justice in the other. The work is also known as the ‘King of Injustice’

Article Title: US suspends 8 tech firms from PERM process: Full list and what it means
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump.

The US administration has suspended eight major technology companies from the employment-based green card process, leaving thousands of foreign professionals, including Indian IT workers, facing uncertainty over their permanent residency plans.The companies named in the October 8 order are Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The US Department of Labor said it would neither accept new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications involving these firms nor process pending ones.The administration has cited alleged abuse of employment-based immigration programmes and the need to protect American workers. US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of laying off American workers while seeking H-1B approvals and green cards for foreign employees. Cognizant had also faced a suspension of its US green card filings in September amid a probe into possible visa fraud.PERM is a key step in obtaining many employer-sponsored green cards. It requires employers to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, willing and available American workers for a position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.The suspension does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards. However, employees with pending PERM applications could face delays, while those whose employers have not yet filed applications may be unable to begin the usual process through these companies. Workers whose PERM certifications have already been approved are in a different position, as the order does not automatically invalidate existing approvals.The decision could create additional uncertainty for H-1B workers approaching the standard six-year limit, particularly those relying on their green card process to qualify for extensions. Some employees may explore sponsorship through another employer, but applications do not automatically transfer when workers change jobs.The duration of the suspension remains uncertain. JD Vance said it would continue “as long as it needs to”. The affected companies could also challenge the decision in federal court. The impact on individual workers will depend on the status of their immigration cases and the length of the suspension.
Article Summary: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini named. US Department of Labor said it would neither accept new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications involving these firms nor process pending ones.

Article Title: A 21-year-old Tennessee moviegoer noticed an 80-year-old AMC usher emptying trash after a screening and hoped a TikTok fundraiser might bring in $500; strangers donated more than $146,000 in less than
Article Text:
Brooklyn Green spotted an elderly worker emptying rubbish at an AMC theatre in Tennessee and recorded a video of her.

Mary, the 80-year-old cinema worker

Mixed reactions to fundraiser

Mary reacts to fundraiser

A 21-year-old woman in Tennessee, United States raised more than $146,000 in less than 24 hours for an 80-year-old cinema worker after noticing her cleaning up rubbish at an AMC theatre. What began as a TikTok video and a small fundraising effort soon attracted thousands of people online, with donations far exceeding the $500 the young woman had initially hoped to collect.According to WVLT, Brooklyn Green had gone to watch a film with her grandparents at the AMC theatre in Maryville, Tennessee, when she noticed an elderly employee pushing a cleaning cart and emptying rubbish. The woman was working hard, and Green decided to record a short video of her.“I just saw her work ethic. She was just working really hard,” Green told WVLT. She later posted the video on TikTok and created a GoFundMe campaign to help the worker, hoping she could eventually enjoy retirement.Green initially expected that friends and family might contribute around $500. Instead, the video spread rapidly, and donations crossed $100,000 within the first day. The total eventually reached approximately $146,000 before Green returned to the theatre to surprise the woman.After launching the fundraiser, Green returned to the theatre to find the elderly employee. However, the woman was not working that day. Green spoke to a manager and learnt that her name was Mary.According to the report, Mary had worked in theatres for more than 45 years. Managers told Green that she enjoyed her job and did not want to stop working. They said Mary was concerned that things might go downhill for her if she stopped working at her age.Green also learnt that Mary regularly helped other people. According to the information shared with her, Mary supported her church and people experiencing homelessness.Her willingness to help others became another reason Green wanted the fundraising effort to succeed. Green recalled a conversation with Mary about the people she supported.“She told me that she helps a mother and child and some of the homeless, and I told her that it comes back tenfold,” Green said.As the TikTok video gained attention, Green began sharing updates about the fundraising campaign. In one update, she explained that Mary was unaware of the video and the money being collected for her.Green also told followers that Mary might not want to accept the donations. According to the manager, Mary was reluctant to stop working, and Green acknowledged that the elderly woman might choose to give the money to other people or charities.The possibility prompted criticism from some social media users. They questioned whether the donations should be returned if Mary did not want the money or decided against retirement.Green responded by making it clear that Mary would have complete control over the funds. "Guys, I said she will decide regardless what to do with the donations. If she decides to give it to a charity or whatever then that is her decision. She is getting every penny, deep breaths lol," Green wrote.She also acknowledged that some people had criticised her for starting the campaign without first speaking to Mary about retirement. "I have gotten a lot of support, but also a lot of backlash for assuming she wants to retire, as well as her not being aware that I was doing this," Green told Storyful, according to CBS News.Despite the criticism, Green continued with her plan to meet Mary and personally tell her about the donations. Green eventually returned to the AMC theatre while Mary was working and surprised her with news of the fundraising campaign.By then, donations had reached approximately $146,000. Green showed Mary the amount on a tablet, revealing how much money strangers had contributed after watching the TikTok video.Mary was overwhelmed by the response and thanked everyone who had donated.“Thank you so very much to all the wonderful people that have donated money. I’m overwhelmed and certainly blessed by the Lord and you wonderful people,” Mary told WVLT.Following the surprise, Mary asked for the GoFundMe campaign to be paused. She said she had already received more than she could ask for. Meanwhile, Green has decided she will work on other projects intended to support more people.
Article Summary: Brooklyn Green, 21, recorded a video of an elderly worker at an AMC theatre in Tennessee. She posted the video on TikTok and created a GoFundMe campaign to help the worker, hoping she could eventually enjoy retirement. Green initially expected that friends and family might contribute around $500. Instead, the video spread rapidly, and donations crossed $100,000 within the first day.

Article Title: A $132,000 GoFundMe was raised for radio host Ronn Owens; federal review found thousands spent on mortgages, businesses and family transfers
Article Text:
Longtime Bay Area radio legend Ronn Owens. Image Credit: The Mercury News

What happened to the $132,000 Ronn Owens GoFundMe donations

Ronn Owens at the KGO studio. Image Credit: The Jewish News of Northern Carolina

The federal review found most spending went elsewhere

Image Credit: SFist

Why did the bankruptcy case become part of the dispute

The court also examined family transfers and other expenses

What did the judge decide about the bankruptcy

The fundraising questions remain separate from criminal charges

A $132,000 GoFundMe campaign created amid radio host Ronn Owens’ health problems became the focus of a federal review after he and his wife sought bankruptcy protection. Court records examined by the US Trustee showed that only about $17,000 of the money was used for medical and pharmacy expenses, while much larger amounts went towards mortgage payments, contributions to businesses and other spending. The review did not result in criminal charges against Owens or his wife, but it raised concerns about whether donors received what they expected from the campaign.The GoFundMe campaign was launched in January 2025 as Owens faced serious health problems. The longtime KGO radio host had described living with Parkinson’s disease for 23 years, along with four bouts of cancer, including colon cancer, and serious heart issues. The campaign appealed to people familiar with his long broadcasting career and said donations would help Owens and his family through difficult circumstances.According to TheDesk, GoFundMe ultimately paid Owens and his wife, Elizabeth Naylor, $132,480 from the campaign. The US Trustee Program in Phoenix later reviewed more than 18 months of financial records, including the bank account into which the donations were deposited.The examination found that the money was largely spent on expenses unrelated to medical care.The figures examined by the trustee provide the clearest picture of how the money was used. TheDesk reported that around $17,000 went towards medical-related bills, although it was not clear whether all of those expenses were connected specifically to Owens’ cancer treatment. By contrast, $118,898 was identified as spending unrelated to medical needs.More than $61,600 went towards mortgage payments, while nearly $44,400 was recorded as capital contributions to companies owned by Owens. The remaining spending included travel, subscriptions and cash given to a child. SFist also reported that other money went towards credit card bills and transfers to family members.The amounts were significant because the campaign had been presented against the backdrop of Owens’ worsening health and financial difficulties. The trustee’s review looked beyond the original fundraising appeal and followed the money through the couple’s accounts.The GoFundMe spending came under scrutiny during Owens and Naylor’s bankruptcy proceedings. The couple first sought Chapter 13 bankruptcy protection, but later filed under Chapter 11 after the earlier case did not provide the protection they sought. Their bankruptcy proceedings eventually brought their financial records under closer examination.SFist reported that during the period covered by the review, the family had more than $20,000 in monthly income and spent more than $520,000 from its bank accounts. The trustee found that only a relatively small portion of the couple’s financial burden was connected to medical expenses.The US Trustee then argued that the bankruptcy case should be dismissed. TheDesk reported that the trustee’s attorney pointed to the bank and GoFundMe records when assessing the couple’s ability to meet Chapter 11 requirements. The court ultimately agreed that there was no reasonable likelihood of a successful reorganisation.Another part of the financial review concerned money transferred to Owens’ daughter, Laura Owens. RadarOnline reported that financial records showed $19,608 in gifts to her, despite the couple having stated under oath that they had not made gifts worth more than $600 per person during the relevant period.The records also showed spending on consumer credit cards, retail and online purchases and other non-medical expenses. RadarOnline noted that the government did not bring criminal or civil fraud charges against Owens or Naylor, and they were not formally accused of fraud in court.The family transfers received additional attention because Laura Owens had her own legal and financial troubles. RadarOnline reported that she had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, which was later dismissed, while SFist described her as financially dependent on her parents. Those circumstances formed part of the wider financial background examined during the bankruptcy proceedings.The federal bankruptcy court ultimately dismissed Owens and Naylor’s case and prevented them from filing another bankruptcy action for at least two years. TheDesk reported that Chief US Bankruptcy Judge Madeleine Wanslee cited significant failures to meet Chapter 11 requirements, along with multiple errors and misstatements in the record.The judge also pointed to changes in sworn statements concerning ownership of the home where the couple lived. Naylor agreed to the two-year restriction but disputed the suggestion that the documents and testimony demonstrated wrongdoing. According to TheDesk, she said she was grateful for the donations and had worked with the court in the interest of transparency.The ruling did not determine that the GoFundMe spending itself amounted to criminal wrongdoing. Instead, the judge allowed donors to pursue possible claims against Owens and Naylor in state court. Creditors were also allowed to resume collection efforts.The federal trustee said the financial records raised a serious question about whether GoFundMe donors received what they believed they were supporting. SFist reported that the trustee did not conclude that a law had been broken. The issue of whether the fundraising appeal and subsequent spending created legal claims was left for donors and GoFundMe to pursue outside the bankruptcy case.The campaign itself remained online at the time of SFist’s August 3 report and had raised about $137,000 against a $140,000 goal.
Article Summary: A GoFundMe campaign created amid radio host Ronn Owens’ health problems became the focus of a federal review after he and his wife sought bankruptcy protection. Court records examined by the US Trustee showed that only about $17,000 of the money was used for medical and pharmacy expenses. Much larger amounts went towards mortgage payments, contributions to businesses and other spending. The review did not result in criminal charges against Owens or his wife, but it raised concerns about whether donors received what they expected from the campaign.

Article Title: Flydubai cockpit attack: Israel to honour Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with top civilian bravery award
Article Text:
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar to receive Israel’s Presidential Award for Civil Heroism

Six Israeli passengers honoured for thwarting attack

What happened aboard the flydubai flight?

Netanyahu had invited pilot to Israel's Independence Day event

Israel will honour Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar with the Presidential Award for Civil Heroism for his role in preventing a major aviation disaster aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, President Isaac Herzog announced on Thursday.Herzog made the announcement while presenting the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism to six Israeli passengers who helped thwart the alleged attempt to crash flight FZ1073 last week.The ceremony was held in Jerusalem.“Alongside the Israeli heroes we honor today, we send our heartfelt wishes for a full and speedy recovery to Captain Smit Machchhar of India. Captain Machchhar’s courage, bravery and professionalism helped prevent this catastrophe,” Herzog said.“Once he regains his strength, it will be an honour and a privilege for me to present him, on behalf of the people of Israel, with the Presidential State of Israel Award for Civil Heroism,” he added.The announcement came as Machchhar continued to recover in a hospital in Abu Dhabi after sustaining serious injuries during an alleged attack by his co-pilot inside the aircraft's cockpit.Herzog presented the civilian heroism award to Tali Manes, Zvika Manes, Yaniv Hayoun, Dr Shota Musayev, Asaf Rajuan and Or Pardilov for their roles in preventing the alleged hijacking attempt, according to The Jerusalem Post and The Times of Israel.Tali Manes was credited with first raising the alarm, while Hayoun, Zvika Manes, Pardilov and Rajuan helped subdue the co-pilot after he allegedly attacked the captain. Musayev, a doctor, provided medical assistance to the injured pilot.“Today we gather in Jerusalem to honour six seemingly ordinary Israelis who proved to be extraordinary human beings, true heroes, by saving the flight last week,” Herzog said.“Thanks to their courage, determination and remarkable presence of mind, these heroes prevented a devastating aviation disaster that would have shocked the entire world and saved 174 precious lives.”The Israeli president also expressed gratitude to the replacement pilots who took over the aircraft and other passengers who helped during the emergency.Herzog said the passengers' actions could not remove the need for a full investigation into the incident.“The civilian bravery and resourcefulness demonstrated by the heroes gathered here cannot absolve us of the obligation to obtain full answers,” he said.The incident occurred last week aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was carrying 174 passengers to Israel. The co-pilot, identified as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, allegedly attacked Machchhar with a crash axe inside the cockpit and attempted to take control of the aircraft.The aircraft transmitted emergency signals and made a rapid descent of more than 17,000 feet, from 34,000 feet, before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The UAE subsequently classified the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.Machchhar received initial treatment in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, before being shifted to Abu Dhabi for further medical care.Ministry of external affairs said on Tuesday that the pilot was recovering well and responding positively to treatment. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the Indian embassy in the UAE was in regular contact with Machchhar, his family and hospital authorities.“Captain Smit Machchhar is in the hospital in Abu Dhabi. Our embassy in the UAE has been in regular touch with him, with his family, with local authorities, and with the hospital authorities. He's recuperating well. He's responding well. And his health is improving,” Jaiswal said.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had earlier spoken to Machchhar while he was receiving treatment in the UAE and praised his actions during the incident.Netanyahu invited the Indian pilot and Prime Minister Narendra Modi to light a flame at Israel's Independence Day event, describing Machchhar as a hero of Israel, India and the world.“It's our highest honour that we give on our Independence Day. It's usually reserved for Israeli citizens, but I think here in this case, all the citizens of Israel will embrace you. They do now, and they will then too. So we hope to see you very soon in Israel,” Netanyahu told the pilot.The Israeli president's announcement on Thursday means Machchhar will also receive a civilian heroism award once he has recovered sufficiently to travel.Herzog established the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.The award recognises civilians who display extraordinary courage while putting themselves at genuine risk to save others.
Article Summary: Six Israeli passengers honoured for thwarting attack on flydubai flight. Indian pilot Smit Machchhar to receive Israel’s Presidential Award for Civil Heroism. President Isaac Herzog presented the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism to six Israeli passengers who helped thwart the alleged attempt to crash flight FZ1073.

Article Title: A 70-year-old woman swam 20 miles across California's Catalina Channel after her brother received a kidney transplant; she raised over €15,000
Article Text:
PC: Irish Kidney Association

How did the 70-year-old woman swim Catalina Channel

Why did Martin Twomey need a kidney transplant

PC: idonate

How difficult was Maura’s Catalina Channel swim

How much did Maura raise for the Irish Kidney Association

Maura Twomey, a 70-year-old former primary school teacher who lives in Boston, crossed California's Catalina Channel on 17 August in an unofficial time of 15 hours, 45 minutes and 23 seconds, pending ratification. She became the oldest person to complete the crossing and earned the Triple Crown of Open Water Swimming. She swam in honour of her youngest brother, Martin, who received a kidney from a deceased donor in June after two and a half years on dialysis. Her fundraising page shows €17,022 raised online for the IKA against a target of €15,000.According to the Irish Kidney Association, Maura Twomey is a native of Ireland who lives in Boston and finished the Catalina Channel crossing on 17 August in an unofficial time of 15:45:23, pending ratification. The swim made her the oldest person to complete the crossing, and it also earned her the Triple Crown of Open Water Swimming, which consists of the English Channel, the 20 Bridges Swim and the Catalina Channel.Her open-water career began with a swim from Alcatraz around her 50th birthday. She then completed the English Channel in 2015, swimming from England to France in 16 hours and 23 minutes at the age of 59. She followed this eight years later with the 20 Bridges Swim around Manhattan in 9 hours and 19 minutes.Martin Twomey, now 60, is the youngest of 14 siblings, and Maura is the seventh eldest. He was born in Dublin, spent his early years in Walkinstown, and moved with his family to Blarney, Co. Cork, when he was five. He now lives in Douglas, Co. Cork, close to his four adult sons, Darren, Daniel, Conor and Liam, and his two grandchildren, Beth (13) and Harry (16). He had built a transport business with a fleet of 30 buses and stepped back from it last year because he was no longer well enough to run it.Martin's wife, Catherine, died from a brain aneurysm in 2023, and he agreed to donate her organs and heart valves. Six months later, his kidney function had deteriorated to the point where he needed to start haemodialysis. He spent two and a half years on dialysis at Cork University Hospital before receiving a kidney from a deceased donor in June this year. The transplant took place at Beaumont Hospital.Several family members, including Maura, offered to donate a kidney as living donors, but Martin declined. He was concerned that a donor might one day need their remaining kidney, or that another family member might need it. Maura Twomey is quoted by the IKA as saying: "Martin always put the welfare of his family before his own."Maura described the swim as every bit as demanding as she had expected. She said: "The swim began in 12-knot winds, chop and swells that never completely settled." She added that in the final hours the winds rose to approximately 20 knots, pushing her off course. She said that whenever she felt she had nothing left, she thought of Martin and what he had endured on dialysis.She made the crossing aboard the Kamryn Dawson, supported by crew chief Elaine Howley and crew member and support swimmer Barbara Cocci. Kayak support was provided by Sidney Russell and Angela Lee, while David Sundius and Joel Virgil served as official observers for the Catalina Channel Swimming Federation. Reaching land meant scrambling up a rocky shoreline to complete the swim, which left her with a skinned knee. She credits Cork-based swim coach Eilis Burns, whom she approached in 2015 when she set out to swim the English Channel.Maura chose to fundraise for Irish Kidney Association CLG, and all funds raised there go directly to the cause. The page records a total of €17,022 raised against a target of €15,000, all of it from online donations. It lists the fundraiser as completed, with donations available until 4 September 2026. The top donors shown are Martin Twomey with €1,000, Mr O'Connor with €502 and Derry Cronin with €500.IKA is working to meet the needs of people and their families living with and affected by end-stage kidney disease, on dialysis and post-transplant. It states that funds from donations and fundraisers provide services such as counselling, financial aid, the use of a patient support centre and patient holidays. Maura says: "The generosity of donor families is extraordinary." She hopes to encourage more people to talk to their families about organ donation
Article Summary: Maura Twomey, a 70-year-old former primary school teacher who lives in Boston, crossed California's Catalina Channel on 17 August. She became the oldest person to complete the crossing and earned the Triple Crown of Open Water Swimming. She swam in honour of her youngest brother, Martin, who received a kidney from a deceased donor in June after two and a half years on dialysis.

Article Title: A Washington farmer who returned to his family farm in 1984 is challenging $618,000 in irrigation penalties after the state Supreme Court heard his case
Article Text:
Photo credit: Mia Ring/Pacific Legal Foundation

How the dispute began

Why the penalties reached $618,000

The case has reached the Washington Supreme Court, which heard arguments on October 1, 2026.

What the farmer says the state should have done

What the courts have ruled so far

A family farm reduced to 290 acres

A Washington farmer who returned to his family’s farm in 1984 is challenging a long-running dispute with the state Department of Ecology after penalties over irrigation threatened the future of his agricultural business. Ron Fodé and his wife, Robin, say the agency refused to help them find a lawful way to irrigate their crops before imposing penalties that originally totalled $618,000. The case has reached the Washington Supreme Court, which heard arguments on October 1, 2026. At its centre is a question about whether the state agency followed a law requiring it to provide technical assistance to water users before moving to penalties.As reported by The Spokesman-Review, Ron and Robin Fodé wrote that the dispute had nearly destroyed their business. The couple said they once farmed 4,000 acres of owned and leased land but now lease just 290 acres. According to the Pacific Legal Foundation, the public-interest legal organisation representing Ron Fodé, the case also raises questions about whether government agencies can enforce unpublished internal policies that affect people’s legal rights.Ron Fodé grew up on the family farm in Grant County, Washington. He took over its operations in 1984 when his father began experiencing health problems. He and Robin raised their four children on the farm, which grew to cover about 4,000 acres at its peak. The dispute began in 2017, when Fodé needed sufficient water rights to irrigate farmland he owned and leased, including fields used to grow potatoes. Under Washington law, farmers generally need legal water rights to withdraw groundwater for irrigation. State law also allows water users to apply for seasonal transfers, which can temporarily shift water rights from one property to another.According to the Washington Court of Appeals’ 2022 ruling, Fodé applied for a seasonal change in January 2017. On February 14, a state watermaster told him that his request had been denied and that he should not irrigate the affected parcels. Fodé maintained that other water-transfer options were available and that he wanted to find a lawful way to continue watering his crops. However, according to The Spokesman-Review, the Department of Ecology refused to accept another application because he had missed an internal February 15 deadline.Fodé and his wife said the deadline had not been adopted through a public rulemaking process and that the agency had not given them access to a permitting process that could have helped them comply with the law. The Department of Ecology subsequently issued cease-and-desist orders directing Fodé and the landowners from whom he leased farmland to stop irrigating without adequate water rights.Fodé continued irrigating during the 2017 growing season. The Department of Ecology later issued penalties covering 103 days of irrigation. According to the Washington Court of Appeals’ ruling, the original penalties comprised $206,000 for irrigation on land Fodé owned, $103,000 for a 65-acre property and $309,000 for 335 acres leased from another landowner. The combined amount was $618,000. The penalties were initially issued jointly to Fodé and his landlords, but the agency later withdrew the penalties against the landlords, leaving Fodé solely liable for the amounts imposed on the three parcels.Fodé did not dispute that he lacked adequate water rights for the disputed irrigation. Instead, he argued that the penalties were invalid because the agency had failed to provide the technical assistance required by state law before imposing them. In June 2019, the Pollution Control Hearings Board upheld some of the penalties but reduced the total from $618,000 to $260,000. The dispute continued through further legal proceedings.Washington law requires the Department of Ecology to provide technical assistance to help water users identify lawful ways to comply, where applicable, before proceeding with enforcement. In their guest opinion in The Spokesman-Review, Ron and Robin Fodé argued that the agency had failed to meet that obligation. They wrote that lawmakers had recognised the complexity of the state’s water regulations and had passed a law in 2002 requiring the agency to provide technical assistance before imposing penalties. According to the couple, the agency should have helped them identify a lawful water-transfer option rather than rejecting their application because of an internal deadline.Their opinion also quoted a regional water resources programme manager at the Department of Ecology as saying, “That’s just something we didn’t do,” when asked why the agency had not provided the assistance they said the law required. The Fodés argue that the February 15 deadline effectively blocked them from applying for a seasonal transfer, even though it had not been formally adopted through a public process. They say the case is therefore about more than the penalties against their farm: it concerns whether agencies can impose rules affecting the public without following the required legal procedures. The Department of Ecology’s position and the legal questions must be assessed through the court proceedings; the couple’s guest opinion presents their account of the dispute.The Washington Court of Appeals addressed part of the dispute in a ruling dated May 12, 2022. It held that Fodé’s appeals against the cease-and-desist orders were timely under the relevant statutory definition of when an agency decision is received.
